The Private Label Opportunity in Matcha

The specialty tea powder market is growing fast, and for food brands, health businesses, and café chains, that growth creates a compelling opportunity: private label matcha products that carry your brand but leverage the production expertise, sourcing relationships, and quality controls of an established wholesale supplier.

Private label matcha is not a new concept — private labeling has been standard practice across food and beverage manufacturing for decades — but it's increasingly accessible to smaller brands and café operators. Today, a café group with five locations, a health food brand with an established e-commerce following, or a fitness company wanting a branded matcha supplement product can realistically develop and launch a private label matcha product without enormous capital investment or manufacturing infrastructure.

What Private Label Matcha Actually Means

Private label in the context of matcha means: you sell a matcha product under your own brand name, on your own packaging, at your own price point — but the actual matcha inside is sourced, quality-controlled, and often packaged by a specialist wholesale supplier on your behalf.

The degree of customization varies by arrangement. At the simpler end, private label means a wholesale supplier fills your branded bags with their standard matcha product. At the more sophisticated end, you can specify the origin, grade, blend, and flavor profile — working with the supplier to develop something that's genuinely differentiated from anything they sell under their own brand.

The private label matcha program at Pure Matcha Partners supports businesses across this full range — from simple brand packaging to custom product development.

Who Private Label Matcha Is For

Private label matcha makes sense for a specific type of business — one that has already validated customer demand for matcha products, has a brand identity worth putting on premium packaging, and wants to build a recurring product revenue stream rather than simply reselling another brand's products.

Café chains and multi-location operators: if you're running three or more café locations and selling significant volumes of matcha, private labeling your matcha creates brand equity, eliminates retail competition (customers can't buy your exact product elsewhere), and often improves margin. Selling small bags of your branded matcha at the counter is also an additional revenue stream.

Health and wellness brands: matcha is extremely well-aligned with health and wellness brand positioning. If you're already selling supplements, health foods, or wellness products, a branded matcha powder fits naturally into that product range.

E-commerce food brands: a private label matcha opens access to high-search-volume matcha keywords and a large, growing customer base. The subscription potential for matcha — customers buying the same product monthly — is strong.

Specialty food retailers: independent delicatessens, health food shops, and specialty food stores can differentiate their matcha offering from major brands by commissioning their own private label product.

The Product Development Process

How does it actually work, from initial interest to product on shelf?

Discovery and brief: the starting point is understanding what you want the product to be — grade, origin, flavor profile, packaging size and format, target consumer, price point. A good private label partner will guide you through this conversation. Contact us to start that conversation.

Sample development: you'll receive samples of proposed matcha options for evaluation. Taste them, assess them in your target application, and provide feedback. This iterative process typically requires two to four rounds before a specification is locked.

Packaging design: your responsibility is typically the artwork and brand design; the supplier handles printing and filling. At minimum, you'll need print-ready artwork files in the correct format.

All matcha grades are potentially available for private label programs — ceremonial, latte grade, and culinary — depending on your target application and customer base.

Minimum order quantities: private label programs typically require higher minimums than standard wholesale to cover packaging setup costs and production runs. Understand the MOQ clearly before committing, and make sure it's consistent with your realistic sales projections.

The Business Case: When Does Private Label Make Economic Sense?

The economics of private label matcha work well when you have: sufficient volume to make the MOQ sensible (you don't want to be sitting on six months of stock), a distribution channel or customer base that generates recurring demand, and a brand positioning that supports a premium price point.

At its best, private label matcha creates a branded product with significantly better margin than reselling another brand's product, while building customer loyalty to your brand rather than to a supplier's brand. The customer who loves your café's branded "house matcha" and buys a bag to take home is a different relationship than the one who picks up a retail bag from a generic supplier.

Use our bulk matcha wholesale program as a starting point to understand volume economics before committing to private label packaging investment.

What to Ask a Private Label Matcha Supplier

Not all suppliers offering private label matcha programs are offering the same thing. Key questions to clarify:

What is the minimum order quantity per SKU, and what does that look like in shelf life terms given my expected monthly sales velocity?

What is the typical lead time from order placement to delivery of finished packaged product?

Who is responsible for compliance with EU food labeling regulations, allergen declarations, and nutrition labeling? This is a non-trivial area where you need clear responsibility allocation.

Can the specification be maintained consistently across repeat orders? What is the process if a harvest produces matcha that doesn't meet your spec?

What certifications are available — organic, non-GMO — and what documentation do you provide?

Is Private Label Matcha Right for Your Brand Right Now?

The honest answer depends on where your business is. If you're a single-location café with stable but modest matcha sales, the MOQ commitment and packaging costs of private label probably don't make sense yet. Focus on building volume with wholesale matcha first, and revisit private label when you're moving enough product to justify the investment.

If you're a growing brand with a genuine distribution platform and a clear brand identity that a private label matcha would reinforce, the timing may be exactly right. The matcha category is growing, differentiation is valuable, and brands that establish their matcha presence now will benefit from first-mover advantages as the market matures.

Start the Conversation

Private label matcha programs are developed through relationship and dialogue — not through a standard order form. The best starting point is to taste the products, understand the volume economics, and have an honest conversation about where your brand is and where it wants to go.

Request a sample to start evaluating the underlying products. Request a quote to understand the wholesale and private label economics. And when you're ready to talk through the specifics, contact us directly — we'll work with you to figure out whether private label is the right move for your business right now, and if it is, exactly how to make it work.

Rooibos: The Caffeine-Free Latte Worth Taking Seriously

If you've dismissed rooibos as just another herbal tea bag, it's time to revisit that assessment. Rooibos (pronounced ROY-boss) is a South African shrub — Aspalathus linearis — whose needle-like leaves produce one of the most distinctive and versatile tea flavors available. Naturally caffeine-free, richly flavored, and loaded with antioxidants, rooibos has been a beloved drink in South Africa for generations. Its moment in the international specialty café scene has been slower than matcha's, but it's arriving.

The rooibos latte — rooibos powder whisked with hot water and topped with steamed milk — is a genuinely excellent drink. The flavor is warm, slightly earthy, sweet with vanilla and honey notes, and uniquely comforting. It pairs beautifully with milk. It works across hot and cold preparations. And as a fully caffeine-free option, it serves a customer segment that's genuinely underserved in most cafés.

What Does Rooibos Actually Taste Like?

Rooibos has a flavor that's often described as sweet, earthy, and slightly woody, with natural vanilla and honey undertones. There's a distinctive quality that's hard to compare directly to other teas — it's not grassy like green tea, not bitter like black tea, not roasted like hojicha. It's its own thing.

The sweetness is notable: rooibos has a naturally sweet character without any added sugar, which makes it an excellent base for drinks where you want sweetness without caloric additions. The earthiness gives it body and depth. The vanilla notes make it extremely compatible with milk, particularly oat milk and whole milk.

In powder form, rooibos is concentrated into an intensely flavored, easy-to-use format. A small amount of rooibos tea powder produces a strongly flavored base for a drink, which keeps per-drink cost very competitive.

The Rooibos Latte Recipe: Step by Step

For one 12oz serving: 3–4 grams of rooibos tea powder, 30–40ml of hot water at 80°C, 200–220ml of steamed milk, and optional honey or light syrup to taste.

Sift the rooibos powder into your preparation bowl or cup. Pour the hot water over the powder. Water temperature for rooibos can be slightly higher than for matcha — around 80°C works well, as rooibos has no chlorophyll to scorch. Whisk vigorously until fully dissolved and smooth. The result is a deep reddish-brown liquid with a rich aroma.

Add sweetener if desired — honey is the most natural pairing and really brings out rooibos's own honey notes. Steam your milk to a smooth microfoam. Pour the steamed milk over the rooibos base. Serve in a transparent glass or a bowl to show off the warm amber-red color.

For a warming variation, stir a small amount of cinnamon into the rooibos paste before adding milk. This creates a deeply comforting, spiced drink that works beautifully in autumn and winter.

The Iced Rooibos Latte: A Summer Staple

Follow the same paste preparation as above. Fill a tall glass with ice, add cold milk, and pour the rooibos paste over or through the milk. The rich amber-red color of rooibos against white milk and clear ice creates a visually appealing drink.

For a flavored variation, add a splash of vanilla syrup and a sprinkle of cinnamon to the paste before combining with cold milk. This version is rich and dessert-like — excellent as an afternoon drink.

Rooibos also works well in cold brew concentrate format: steep rooibos powder in cold water for 8–12 hours, strain, and use as a concentrate base for iced drinks with milk added to order.

Why Rooibos Belongs on Your Specialty Drinks Menu

The case for adding a rooibos latte comes down to three things: caffeine-free status, flavor appeal, and customer differentiation.

Caffeine-free is increasingly important. A growing segment of café customers actively seeks non-caffeinated options — pregnant customers, those with caffeine sensitivity, late-afternoon visitors who want a warm drink without disrupting sleep. Coffee-based decaf is an option, but many customers prefer to avoid coffee entirely. Matcha is caffeinated. Hojicha is low-caffeine but not caffeine-free. Caffeine-free specialty powders like rooibos fill a genuine gap.

Flavor appeal is broad. Unlike more acquired tastes like matcha, rooibos is immediately accessible to a wide range of customers. The naturally sweet, gently earthy flavor is pleasant to almost everyone on first try.

Menu differentiation: few cafés currently serve a dedicated rooibos latte. Being one of the first in your area to put a well-made rooibos latte on your permanent menu is an easy point of difference for an affordable cost.

For more inspiration on low-caffeine specialty drinks, see also our guide on what is hojicha — another excellent option that complements rooibos on a seasonally balanced specialty menu.

Rooibos in Food and Baking Applications

Rooibos powder works in food applications beyond drinks. Rooibos shortbread has a distinctive warm flavor that's excellent with cream cheese or lemon glazes. Rooibos panna cotta or custard highlights the natural vanilla and honey notes beautifully. Rooibos in chocolate is a surprisingly compelling combination — the earthiness of rooibos complements dark chocolate without fighting it.

For food manufacturers looking for a caffeine-free specialty ingredient for functional beverages, snack bars, or wellness products, rooibos powder is worth serious consideration. The caffeine-free, antioxidant-rich profile supports health positioning, and the distinctive flavor profile differentiates products on shelf.

Sourcing Rooibos Tea Powder for Commercial Use

Quality rooibos powder should have a deep reddish-brown color (not pale or washed-out), a strong, clean rooibos aroma, a sweet-earthy flavor with no off-notes, and fine particle size for smooth dissolution. Organic certification is available for rooibos grown under certified standards in South Africa's Cederberg region, where the best quality rooibos is produced.

Jasmine Tea: A Classic Flavor in a Modern Format

Jasmine tea is one of the most beloved tea traditions in the world, with a history stretching back over a thousand years in China. The pairing of green tea and jasmine flowers produces something genuinely magical: a floral, delicate, slightly sweet flavor that's instantly recognizable and universally appealing. It's one of the most popular tea flavors globally, and for good reason.

Jasmine tea powder brings that classic flavor into a modern, versatile format that works across the full spectrum of café and food service applications. Where traditional jasmine tea requires brewing time and produces a delicate liquid, jasmine tea powder creates a concentrated flavor base that integrates instantly into hot drinks, cold drinks, desserts, and baked goods. For commercial kitchen use, the advantages are significant.

What Is Jasmine Tea Powder?

Jasmine tea powder is made by finely grinding jasmine-scented green tea into a smooth powder, similar in process to how matcha is made. The starting material is green tea that has been scented with fresh jasmine blossoms — a traditional process in which layers of tea and jasmine flowers are alternated, allowing the tea leaves to absorb the floral fragrance over hours or days. Multiple scenting rounds are used for premium products, resulting in a deeply aromatic tea.

The dried, scented tea is then ground into a fine powder, concentrating the jasmine flavor in a format that dissolves readily in liquid. The result has both the character of green tea (some grassiness, a light vegetal quality, natural sweetness) and the pronounced floral notes of jasmine.

Jasmine tea powder wholesale from a specialty supplier ensures consistent flavor intensity and color, with the food-service packaging and supply reliability that a commercial operation needs.

The Jasmine Tea Latte: A Menu Opportunity

The jasmine tea latte is an underutilized menu item in most Western cafés, despite being a genuinely compelling drink. The flavor profile sits at the intersection of floral and creamy — familiar enough to attract mainstream café customers, distinctive enough to offer genuine novelty for people looking beyond the usual coffee-and-matcha menu.

Preparation follows the same basic method as a matcha latte: sift 3–4 grams of jasmine tea powder into a bowl, add 30–40ml of hot water at 70–75°C, whisk into a smooth paste, then top with steamed milk of choice. The resulting drink has a light green-gold color and a beautifully fragrant floral flavor that carries well through milk.

Sweetener recommendations: jasmine tea pairs particularly well with honey or light syrup. The honey-jasmine combination is a classic worth standardizing as your menu preparation. A touch of vanilla also complements the floral notes without overpowering them.

For iced versions, follow the same paste method and serve over ice with cold milk. An iced jasmine green tea latte with honey is an excellent summer menu item that feels fresh, light, and premium.

Beyond Lattes: Jasmine Tea Powder in Food Applications

Jasmine tea powder is a genuinely flexible ingredient once you start experimenting with it. The floral, slightly sweet character works in a surprising range of applications.

Jasmine tea panna cotta or mousse: the delicate flavor infuses beautifully into cream-based desserts without requiring extraction time or straining. Use 5–8 grams per 500ml of cream, taste, and adjust. The floral notes come through clearly in a finished panna cotta.

Jasmine tea cookies and shortbread: the floral character carries well through butter and sugar in baking. Jasmine tea shortbread has a delicate, perfumed quality that makes it a perfect accompaniment to premium tea service.

Jasmine tea cake: add 10–15 grams of jasmine tea powder to a standard genoise or chiffon cake recipe for a beautifully fragrant, pale green-tinged cake. Pair with jasmine tea buttercream for a showstopper product for a premium bakery case.

Jasmine tea cocktails and mocktails: for cafés with evening programs or function catering, jasmine tea powder works in both alcoholic and non-alcoholic drinks. A jasmine tea mocktail with sparkling water, honey syrup, and a squeeze of lemon is a compelling non-alcoholic offering.

Where Jasmine Tea Powder Fits in Your Menu Strategy

Specialty drinks for cafés are increasingly important as café menus expand beyond coffee to attract a wider customer base. Jasmine tea powder is a strong addition to any specialty beverages program for several reasons.

It's familiar but not overexposed. Jasmine tea is a recognizable, loved flavor — most customers know jasmine tea from conventional tea bags or Asian restaurants. But a jasmine tea latte is still novel enough to generate interest and conversation.

It's naturally caffeine-containing and marketed as a premium, wellness-adjacent product in the same space as matcha and green tea. For cafés positioning around health, wellbeing, or East Asian tea culture, jasmine tea fits the narrative perfectly.

It photographs well. The light green-gold color is elegant and distinctive in a latte glass, particularly with a dried jasmine flower garnish.

It works across dayparts. Jasmine tea's relatively moderate caffeine level and light flavor profile make it work for morning, afternoon, and evening drinks alike.

Sourcing Jasmine Tea Powder at Wholesale

The quality of jasmine tea powder depends on two things: the quality of the green tea base and the intensity of the jasmine scenting. Single-scented powders have a lighter, more delicate floral note. Multiple-scented products have a more pronounced, rounded jasmine character that holds up better in milk and baked applications.

For café use, a medium-to-strong jasmine intensity is typically preferable — it needs to be perceptible through milk without requiring excessive dosing.

Ready to Add Jasmine to Your Menu?

Jasmine tea powder requires minimal staff training (same technique as matcha lattes), works in hot and cold applications, and appeals to a wide customer base. It's one of the most accessible specialty powders available for café menus today.

Why Your Matcha Supplier Relationship Matters More Than You Think

Most café owners spend a lot of time thinking about their coffee supplier. The origin, the roast profile, the delivery schedule, the service relationship — these get careful attention because coffee is often the core product around which everything else is built. Matcha deserves the same level of consideration, and for growing numbers of venues, it's becoming nearly as important.

A matcha supplier relationship that works well is one where you rarely think about it. The product arrives consistently, the quality doesn't drift, the spec matches what you've built your recipe around, and when you have questions or issues, you get a real response. A supplier relationship that doesn't work well costs you in customer experience, staff frustration, inconsistent drinks, and eventually revenue.

This guide covers what to actually look for when choosing a wholesale matcha supplier — the criteria that matter in practice, not just the marketing language on their website.

Quality Consistency: The Most Important Factor

Anyone can source a single excellent batch of matcha. The real test of a supplier is whether batch three, six, and ten look, smell, and taste like batch one.

Matcha is a natural agricultural product with inherent seasonal variation. That variation is manageable — but it should be managed by the supplier, not passed on to you as a surprise. A good wholesale supplier maintains a specification for each product they sell: a defined color range, flavor profile, and particle size that they test against each incoming batch. When a batch doesn't meet spec, they don't ship it. When there's meaningful variation, they communicate it proactively.

Ask any supplier you're evaluating: how do you manage batch-to-batch consistency? What testing do you do on each batch? How do you handle variation between harvest seasons? The quality of the answer tells you a lot.

Traceability: Knowing Where Your Matcha Comes From

The matcha market has a serious provenance problem. A meaningful proportion of matcha sold as "Japanese" in Europe comes from China, where production costs are lower but quality standards, farming practices, and heavy metal residue levels can differ significantly. Misrepresentation of origin is a real issue.

For cafés serving health-conscious customers — and matcha customers tend to be exactly that — the ability to verify Japanese origin and organic certification is increasingly important. Customers ask about it. Food journalists write about it. And the reputational risk of serving misleadingly labeled products is real.

A trustworthy supplier should be able to tell you which prefecture in Japan your matcha comes from, which harvest it represents, and whether it carries organic certification. Ideally, they can share testing data for pesticide residue, heavy metals, and microbial safety. Our quality process at Pure Matcha Partners is built around full traceability from Japanese farm to European delivery.

Logistics and Reliability: The Operational Reality

Quality is essential, but operational reliability is what keeps your café running. Key logistics questions: what are the lead times from order to delivery? What are the minimum order quantities? Do they carry adequate stock to fill your order reliably, or are products regularly out of stock? How do they handle urgent orders when you run low unexpectedly?

For most café operators, a supplier who can deliver reliably within 2–5 business days with reasonable minimum order quantities is the practical baseline. If you're a multi-location group or a high-volume single venue, discuss your volume requirements explicitly and get confirmation that the supplier can genuinely support your needs.

Check how products are packaged for transit — nitrogen-flushed, resealable bags are important for shelf life and signal a supplier who takes product quality seriously.

Range: Meeting Your Full Menu Needs

A wholesale matcha supplier worth working with should offer the full range of grades you need — at minimum, latte grade and ceremonial grade matcha for drink applications, and culinary grade for any baking or manufacturing needs. Having a single supplier relationship that covers your whole tea powder range is operationally simpler and often better for pricing.

Beyond matcha, consider whether your supplier carries complementary products you use or are interested in adding: hojicha, specialty tea powders, botanical powders. A supplier with a broader specialty powder range can simplify your procurement significantly.

The matcha for cafés and hospitality page outlines how Pure Matcha Partners specifically supports café and hospitality operators — from product selection to ongoing supply.

Pricing and Value: Getting the Relationship Right

Matcha pricing varies dramatically across the market, and the relationship between price and quality is real but not linear. Very cheap matcha is almost always a quality compromise somewhere — in sourcing, processing, or consistency controls. The right value equation is: the lowest price at which your specific quality requirements are met, with reliable supply and service.

Getting there usually requires tasting several options, understanding what you actually need from a functional standpoint, and then comparing pricing at the volumes relevant to your business. Request a wholesale price list from potential suppliers and compare on a per-gram basis at your actual volume. Volume pricing structures vary significantly — some suppliers offer meaningful discounts at 1kg, others don't scale until 5kg or 10kg.

How to Evaluate a New Matcha Supplier Before Committing

Here's a practical evaluation process for any new supplier.

Request samples first. Any serious B2B supplier will send samples without hesitation. Evaluate those samples rigorously — color, aroma, flavor in water, flavor in milk, and color in milk. Run the tests with your team.

Ask the hard questions: where is this matcha from, specifically? What's the harvest date? What testing has been done? Can you share test reports? These aren't unreasonable questions — they're basic due diligence.

Place a small first order before committing to large volumes. Test one or two delivery cycles to verify logistics performance and confirm that the product you receive matches the sample.

Build the relationship. The best supplier relationships involve ongoing communication about upcoming harvests, new products, and any anticipated supply chain changes. Wholesale matcha supply programs at Pure Matcha Partners are designed around exactly this kind of long-term relationship.

Start with a Sample Pack, Then Discuss Volume

The simplest first step is always the sample. Request a free sample pack and evaluate our products in your own kitchen, with your equipment and your team. If the quality is right, we'll talk wholesale pricing and get a supply program in place that works for your volume and delivery preferences.

What Is Ube and Why Is It Having a Moment?

If you've noticed an increasingly vivid purple spreading across café menus and food social media, that's ube — and it's not going anywhere. Ube (pronounced oo-bay) is a purple yam native to the Philippines with a flavor profile that's genuinely unlike anything else: sweet, subtly nutty, with vanilla and coconut undertones that make it immediately appealing even to customers who've never tried it before.

In the Philippines, ube has been a beloved ingredient in desserts for generations — in halaya (a sweet yam jam), in cakes, in ice cream. Its emergence on the international café and beverage scene is a natural extension of that culinary tradition, powered by the extraordinary visual appeal of that deep purple color and the growing global interest in Filipino food culture.

For café operators and food developers, ube powder is a versatile, high-impact ingredient. The purple latte — an ube powder latte — is one of the most visually striking drinks you can put on a menu, and its flavor profile works across hot, iced, blended, and baked applications.

Understanding Ube Powder vs. Fresh Ube

Fresh ube is a seasonal, perishable root vegetable that requires significant preparation — peeling, cooking, pureeing — before it can be used in any application. That's simply not practical in a commercial café setting.

Ube powder is dehydrated and ground ube yam, providing all the flavor and color benefits of fresh ube in a shelf-stable, easy-to-use format. High-quality ube powder preserves the characteristic color (a deep, vivid purple) and the sweet, slightly earthy, vanilla-adjacent flavor of the fresh yam. It dissolves or blends easily into hot and cold liquids and portions consistently for accurate recipe work.

The operational benefits are clear: no food waste, consistent flavor and color from batch to batch, long shelf life, and simple storage. Ube powder wholesale from a specialty supplier ensures you're getting a food-service-appropriate product with consistent color intensity and flavor.

The Classic Ube Latte Recipe

Here's the base recipe for a hot ube latte.

For one 12oz serving: 15–20 grams of ube powder (adjust to your desired intensity), 30ml hot water at 70–80°C, 200ml steamed milk, and optional simple syrup to taste. Ube powder is naturally sweet, so taste before adding sweetener.

Sift the ube powder into a bowl or small pitcher. Add hot water and whisk vigorously until smooth. The powder should dissolve into a thick, vivid purple paste. Add sweetener here if using. Pour steamed milk over the ube base.

The result is a warm, purple-hued latte with a creamy, sweet, lightly exotic flavor that most customers who try it immediately love. Serve in a clear glass for maximum visual impact.

The Iced Purple Latte: Your Instagram-Ready Summer Drink

The iced ube latte may be the single most visually compelling drink in the specialty beverage world right now. The combination of vivid purple, white milk, and clear ice in a tall glass photographs extraordinarily well.

Follow the same paste preparation as the hot version. Fill a tall glass with ice. Pour cold milk over the ice, then add the ube paste over or beneath the milk — the density difference creates a stunning layered effect that holds for a minute or two before the customer stirs.

Many cafés serve the iced ube latte unstirred with a note to mix before drinking, precisely because the pre-mixed version looks less visually striking than the layered presentation.

Increase the dose slightly for iced versions — use 20–25 grams — to account for dilution from the ice.

Beyond Lattes: Other Ube Menu Applications

Ube in baking opens up an entire world. Ube powder works in cakes, cookies, macarons, mochi, and donuts. A vivid purple ube glazed donut is a guaranteed social media moment. Ube cookies with white chocolate chips are currently popular in specialty bakeries. The color and flavor are distinctive enough to make these products immediately stand out from standard café pastry cases.

Ube smoothies and blended drinks are a natural extension. Blend ube powder with frozen banana, coconut milk, and ice for an ube smoothie. The flavor combination of ube and coconut is a classic Filipino pairing that works beautifully.

Ube soft serve or ice cream is an option for cafés with frozen dessert capabilities. The deep purple color is extraordinary in ice cream form, and the flavor holds up beautifully in a frozen application. Ube also works as a striking flavoring in pancake batters, waffles, and boba drinks.

Positioning Ube on Your Menu

The ube latte works at different price points and for different venue types. In a trendy, visually-led urban café, ube lattes can be priced as premium specialty drinks and marketed heavily through social media. In a more food-led setting — a patisserie, a dessert café, a Filipino-influenced concept — ube can become a signature flavor identity across multiple menu items.

The visual nature of ube-based products makes them unusually strong performers on social media. A single Instagram post of a well-made ube latte or ube cake slice can generate significant discovery traffic if the visual quality is there. This is a genuine marketing advantage for a low cost of goods added to your menu.

Sourcing Ube Powder for Commercial Use

Not all ube powders are equal. Key quality indicators: depth and consistency of purple color, flavor authenticity (natural ube flavor rather than artificial sweetness), fine particle size for smooth dissolution, and food-safe processing appropriate for commercial use.

The Story Behind Ceremonial Grade Matcha

The term "ceremonial grade" is everywhere in the matcha market right now, appearing on products ranging from genuine first-harvest Japanese matcha to budget blends that share almost nothing with the traditional product. Understanding what real ceremonial grade matcha is — where it comes from, why it costs what it costs, and who should actually be buying it — helps you cut through the marketing noise and make purchasing decisions that serve your business.

The "ceremonial" designation refers to the Japanese tea ceremony tradition (chanoyu), a ritual that has been practiced for centuries and that demands the finest possible matcha. In this context, "ceremonial grade" is not just a quality indicator — it's a statement about the entire supply chain behind the product, from the farming practices to the final grind.

What Makes Ceremonial Matcha Different at the Farm Level

The quality difference in ceremonial matcha starts with farming decisions made weeks before harvest. Tea plants destined for ceremonial grade matcha are shaded for a minimum of 20 days, and often 25–30 days, using traditional reed screens or modern synthetic shade cloth. This extended shading period stresses the plants in a specific, beneficial way: they produce more chlorophyll in response to reduced light, which creates both the vivid green color and a dramatic increase in l-theanine content.

L-theanine is the amino acid responsible for the smooth, meditative quality associated with high-quality matcha. It moderates the caffeine response, producing an alert-but-calm state rather than the jittery energy of coffee. In ceremonial grade matcha, l-theanine levels can be three to four times higher than in unshaded green teas.

Only the youngest top leaves — the shinme, or first growth — are selected for ceremonial grade, harvested in the first flush of the season (ichibancha). After harvest, destemming and deveining (tencha processing) removes the fibrous parts that would introduce bitterness. The resulting tencha is then stone-ground at extremely slow speeds on granite mills, generating minimal heat and preserving both the nutrients and delicate flavor compounds.

The Flavor Profile: What to Expect

Ceremonial matcha has a flavor profile that distinguishes it immediately from every other grade. The first note is umami — that deep, savory-sweet richness that Japanese cuisine is famous for, here expressed in tea form. There's a natural sweetness that needs no added sugar. A gentle grassiness that's fresh rather than harsh. And a smooth, lingering finish with no bitterness whatsoever.

The color in the bowl is stunning: a vivid, electric green that's noticeably more intense than latte or culinary grade matcha. The texture when whisked is like liquid silk — uniform, fine, with a light foam that holds beautifully.

For the traditional preparation — a few grams whisked in a chawan with hot water at 70°C — ceremonial matcha needs nothing else. It's complete as it is. Ceremonial Matcha Japan Organic with full farm-level traceability supports a brand narrative that latte or culinary grade simply can't match.

Who Should Be Buying Ceremonial Grade Matcha?

This grade isn't for everyone, and that's not a criticism — it's a practical observation. Here's who ceremonial grade genuinely serves.

Specialty tea cafés and destination tea experiences: if your venue is positioning itself as a premium tea destination — offering traditional matcha preparation, curated tea menus, or a Japanese tea ceremony experience — ceremonial grade is your core product. Customers who seek out this experience know what ceremonial matcha should taste and look like, and they will notice if you substitute a lower grade.

Premium beverage brands using matcha as a hero ingredient: if your product concept centers on the quality and provenance of your matcha, ceremonial grade provides both the quality and the storytelling that justify a premium price point.

High-end cafés adding a premium matcha tier: even if latte grade matcha is your everyday workhorse, a ceremonial grade offering at a premium price point can add a compelling option for your most engaged matcha customers. "Ceremonial grade matcha bowl" as a premium menu item is a credible upsell.

Compare matcha grades in more detail if you want a full breakdown before making your decision.

Who Probably Doesn't Need Ceremonial Grade

Be honest with yourself here. If you're primarily making matcha lattes in a fast-casual café environment, the nuances of ceremonial grade matcha will mostly be lost in the milk. The additional cost per gram won't translate into proportionally more revenue unless you actively market and price the premium drink accordingly.

Food manufacturers using matcha in multi-ingredient formulations should almost always use culinary grade. The flavor complexity of ceremonial grade gets masked by other ingredients, and the cost differential is very difficult to justify.

For most commercial latte programs, well-sourced latte grade matcha outperforms ceremonial in cost-effectiveness without compromising on the drink quality that your customers can actually perceive.

Ceremonial Matcha at Wholesale: What to Know

Bulk matcha ordering at ceremonial grade requires a supplier who can guarantee consistency across harvests. Ceremonial matcha is a seasonal, terroir-driven product — meaning flavor nuances will vary slightly year to year just as wine does. A good wholesale partner will be transparent about those variations and will spec their products clearly.

Storage requirements are strict: cool, dark, and airtight. Ceremonial matcha in an opened bag at room temperature in a warm kitchen will degrade noticeably within a few weeks. If you're using it for a lower-volume premium menu item, portion it into small working quantities and keep the bulk stock sealed.

The best way to understand whether ceremonial grade matcha is right for your business is to put it in a bowl and drink it. The quality difference is immediate and tangible.

Why Most Matcha Lattes Fall Short

You've seen the photos. A vivid green matcha latte, perfectly layered in a glass, steamed milk curling alongside that electric color. It looks effortless. In practice, it's a drink that rewards good technique and punishes shortcuts.

The majority of disappointing matcha lattes come down to one of three things: wrong grade of matcha, wrong water temperature, or skipped technique steps. Get those three elements right and you'll be making café-quality matcha lattes consistently, whether you're behind a commercial bar or developing a recipe for a food service brand.

The Ingredients You'll Need

The ingredient list for a classic matcha latte is short, which is exactly why the quality of each component matters so much.

For one serving (12oz / 350ml): 2.5–3 grams of ceremonial or latte grade matcha powder. If you want to use a premium option, our Premium Matcha Japan Organic produces a greatresult with a noticeably more vivid color and cleaner flavor.

30ml of hot water at 65–70°C. Temperature is critical as hotter than 75°C and you start to affect the chlorophyll, which makes the matcha taste bitter and turns the color dull.

200–220ml of your milk of choice. Oat milk is currently the most popular option in café settings and produces a naturally sweet, creamy result. Barista-formulation plant milks are worth investing in for their steaming and texturing properties.

Optional: 5–10ml of simple syrup or liquid sweetener, added to the cup before topping with milk.

Step-by-Step: The Classic Hot Matcha Latte

Sift your matcha first. Use a fine-mesh tea strainer to sift 2.5-3 grams of latte grade matcha into your bowl, pitcher, or serving cup. Any lumps present at this stage will only get worse when liquid is added.

Add the hot water. Pour your 65-70°C water directly over the sifted matcha. Fully hydrating the powder before adding milk creates a paste that integrates into the drink far more smoothly.

Whisk into a smooth paste. Use a bamboo chasen with rapid W or M shaped strokes, then in circular motions to raise a fine foam. An electric handheld frother also works well in a commercial setting. You're aiming for complete dissolution, no visible powder clumps, and a light frothy surface.

Steam your milk. Heat to 65–68°C and texture it to a microfoam consistency. Let the steamed milk settle for 10 seconds after frothing.

Pour and serve. Add your sweetener to the matcha base if using, then pour the steamed milk over and through the matcha. Serve immediately.

The Iced Matcha Latte: A Slightly Different Method

Prepare the matcha paste exactly as above: sift, hot water, whisk. Don't skip the hot water step even for iced drinks. The hot water is necessary to properly hydrate and dissolve the matcha powder. Trying to dissolve matcha in cold liquid produces persistent clumps.

Fill your glass with ice. Pour the matcha paste over the ice, then pour cold milk directly over. The contrast between the cold milk and the vibrant green matcha paste creates a beautiful visual as it settles. Many cafés serve it un-stirred for maximum visual impact.

Increase your matcha dose slightly for iced versions, so use 3–3.5 grams rather than 2.5 to account for the dilution from melting ice.

Equipment That Makes a Difference

A bamboo chasen (whisk) is the traditional tool and still one of the best for producing a smooth, fully integrated matcha preparation. They're affordable, last hundreds of uses when properly cared for, and produce a distinctive fine foam that electric frothers replicate but don't quite match. Matcha accessories including chasens and chawan are available for cafés wanting to add a visual element to their preparation.

A fine-mesh sieve eliminates the clumping problem before it starts. A temperature-controlled kettle makes hitting the 65–70°C range consistently much easier than guessing. Digital scales for dosing as the difference between 2 grams and 3 grams of matcha in a 12oz drink is noticeable, and training your team to measure rather than scoop pays dividends.

Scaling the Recipe for Commercial Service

In a busy café environment, making matcha paste to order can create bottlenecks during peak service. The professional solution is batch paste preparation.

At the start of each service, prepare a matcha concentrate: whisk 20g of matcha powder with 200ml of hot water at 70°C into a smooth, thick paste. Store in a sealed container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. When an order comes in, portion 20ml of paste per drink (approximately 2g matcha equivalent), add any sweetener, and top with steamed milk. This reduces per-drink preparation time dramatically without compromising quality.

Seasonal Variations Worth Adding to Your Menu

Once your base recipe is dialed in, matcha lattes lend themselves well to seasonal variations that keep your menu feeling fresh. Brown sugar matcha latte (a matcha latte with a syrup made from brown sugar and cinnamon) is enormously popular and works year-round. Lavender matcha latte is a spring and summer variation that photographs beautifully and appeals to the floral-flavored drink trend. Spiced matcha latte with ginger, cardamom, and cinnamon is a natural autumn offering.

For all of these, the base technique remains the same. The variations happen in the sweetener or in an additional flavored syrup added before the milk. Keep the technique consistent and vary the flavoring layer.

Ready to Try the Recipe with Premium Matcha?

The recipe only works as well as the matcha you put in it. If your current matcha isn't producing the color, flavor, and consistency you want, the issue is almost certainly the powder, not the process.

Try our matcha! We ship samples of our latte grade and premium matcha to cafés and food businesses across Europe. Test the recipe with our matcha against your current product and see the difference for yourself.

Two Japanese Tea Powders, Completely Different Experiences

Matcha and hojicha are two of the most compelling Japanese tea powders for café beverage menus — but they're genuinely different products that serve different customer occasions. If you're a café owner or beverage developer trying to decide which to stock, or whether to stock both, this comparison will give you the information you need to make that call confidently.

Both are made from the Camellia sinensis plant, both come in powder form for easy use in drinks and food applications, and both have Japanese craft traditions behind them. Beyond those surface similarities, almost everything about them is different: the production process, the flavor, the color, the caffeine level, the customer appeal, and the optimal use cases.

The Production Difference That Changes Everything

Understanding why matcha and hojicha taste so different starts with the production process.

Matcha is made from shade-grown tea leaves that are carefully steamed, dried, destemmed, and then stone-ground into an ultra-fine powder. The shading process is the key: by blocking sunlight for 20–30 days before harvest, producers dramatically increase chlorophyll and l-theanine content in the leaves. The result is that vivid green color and the characteristic umami, grassy, complex flavor.

Hojicha takes a fundamentally different path. The leaves — typically from later harvests, with more mature stems and stalks included — are roasted at high temperatures, usually around 200°C. That roasting process breaks down chlorophyll (turning the leaves from green to reddish-brown), caramelizes the naturally present sugars, reduces caffeine levels significantly, and creates a whole new set of flavor compounds. The resulting powder is a warm, toasty, caramel-scented product that looks and tastes nothing like matcha.

Flavor Profile: Head-to-Head

This is where the customer-facing difference is most apparent.

Ceremonial matcha has a fresh, vegetal, umami-forward flavor with a natural sweetness and a slightly grassy character. Higher grades have complexity and depth. It's an acquired taste for some, but increasingly mainstream as specialty tea culture grows. Latte grade matcha in a milk drink is bold, green, slightly sweet, and unmistakably matcha.

Hojicha is the opposite sensory experience. It's warm, roasted, nutty, and caramel-like. It's often described as the Japanese equivalent of a warm hug — comforting, smooth, without any grassiness or bitterness. Customers who find matcha too intense or too "green" often love hojicha immediately. It's a much easier entry point into Japanese tea culture for people who are new to it.

In terms of heat — winter lattes — hojicha wins on sheer comfort factor. In terms of that vivid Instagram-ready green visual, matcha wins decisively.

Caffeine Content: A Meaningful Difference for Menu Strategy

This is a practical differentiator that affects how you position these drinks on your menu and what time of day they sell.

Matcha is a moderate-to-high caffeine tea powder. A typical 3g serving of matcha contains roughly 70–105mg of caffeine, depending on the grade and sourcing. That's comparable to a shot of espresso and makes a matcha latte a legitimate morning or afternoon energy drink.

Hojicha powder is low in caffeine. The roasting process degrades caffeine significantly, leaving roughly 7–10mg per gram — so a 3g hojicha latte contains perhaps 20–30mg of caffeine. This makes hojicha an excellent option for evening service, for customers who are caffeine-sensitive or pregnant, for children's menus, and as a late-night café option for customers who want a warm drink without the sleep disruption.

Positioning a hojicha latte as "low caffeine" or "caffeine-conscious" on your menu is a real selling point for a growing segment of café-goers.

Color and Visual Appeal: Green vs. Brown

Let's be direct: matcha wins on visual impact in a way that hojicha simply doesn't replicate. That vivid green matcha latte has become one of the most photographed drinks in the world, and that visual pull drives discovery and social media sharing in a way that directly affects café sales.

Hojicha lattes are attractive in their own right — a warm amber-to-brown color with a creamy milk top is visually appealing, particularly in autumn and winter contexts. But the color story is less dramatic.

For cafés that invest heavily in visual identity and social media presence, matcha has an edge. For venues that prioritize comfort, seasonality, and differentiated menus, hojicha offers a compelling and less saturated visual aesthetic.

Which One Should You Stock?

The strongest argument is: stock both. They're complementary rather than competitive.

Matcha speaks to the morning rush, the health-conscious customer, the aesthetics-driven social media sharer, and the green tea enthusiast. Hojicha speaks to the afternoon or evening visitor, the caffeine-sensitive customer, the winter comfort seeker, and the customer who finds matcha too intense.

Together, they give you a Japanese tea program that covers multiple dayparts and customer personas. They require the same basic preparation technique. And you can trial both easily before committing to volume.

Why Matcha Grading Exists (And Why It's Often Misunderstood)

‍

If you've spent any time sourcing matcha for commercial use, you've encountered the grading terminology: ceremonial, latte grade, culinary. These terms appear on every supplier's website and yet there's no universally regulated definition for any of them. Unlike olive oil, where "extra virgin" has a legal definition with specific chemical standards, matcha grades are largely marketing categories that vary between suppliers.

‍

That doesn't mean the grades are meaningless, actually far from it. It means you need to understand what's actually behind the labels, and what questions to ask when evaluating suppliers. This guide gives you the practical, no-nonsense version: what each grade means, what drives the quality differences, and which grade is right for which application in your business.

‍

What Actually Determines Matcha Quality?

‍

Before diving into the grades, it helps to understand the factors that genuinely drive quality in matcha production. These are the variables that separate excellent matcha from mediocre matcha, regardless of what the label says.

‍

Shading duration is one of the most significant. High-quality matcha comes from tea plants that are covered for 20 to 30 days before harvest. This shading process drives the production of chlorophyll (creating the vivid green color) and l-theanine (an amino acid that contributes to the umami flavor and smooth, calming effect of matcha). Less shading means less l-theanine, less chlorophyll, and a lower-quality product.

‍

Harvest timing matters. The first harvest of the year (ichibancha, typically in late April to early May) produces the youngest, most tender leaves, which is the basis for ceremonial grade matcha. Later harvests yield leaves with higher tannin content and less l-theanine. Stem and vein removal, known as tencha processing, is another quality differentiator. For the finest grades, the dried leaves are destemmed and deveined before grinding.

‍

Ceremonial Grade: The Apex of Matcha Quality

‍

Ceremonial matcha sits at the top of the quality hierarchy. It's made from first-harvest, shade-grown tea leaves that are destemmed, deveined, and ground extremely fine on slow-turning granite stone mills. The particle size is typically under 10 microns, giving it a texture that's almost silky. The color is a vivid, bright green. The flavor is complex: naturally sweet, distinctly umami, with a smooth finish and none of the harsh bitterness you find in lower grades.

‍

Traditional Japanese tea ceremony uses this grade exclusively, which is the origin of the name. The preparation is simple: a few grams whisked with hot water, nothing added. The quality speaks for itself.

‍

In commercial settings, ceremonial grade works for premium straight matcha service, high-end matcha shots, and positioning a café as a destination for serious tea drinkers. It's also the right choice for food brands that want to use matcha as a premium ingredient in products where the marketing story matters as much as the function.

‍

Latte Grade: Purpose-Built for Milk-Based Drinks

‍

Latte grade matcha is where the majority of commercial café usage lives, and for good reason. This grade is specifically developed and sourced to perform in milk-based applications. The leaves are typically from slightly later in the harvest season than ceremonial grade, selected for their bold, assertive flavor in milk. The color is a rich, consistent green. It is not quite as electric as ceremonial, but vivid enough to produce a beautiful, appetizing drink.

‍

The flavor profile of good latte grade matcha is intentionally more robust than ceremonial. It needs to cut through the fat and protein in milk without disappearing. The economics of latte grade are also well-suited to commercial use. You'll use 2–4 grams per drink, potentially dozens of times a day. The price per gram of latte grade is considerably more accessible than ceremonial, making it the practical choice for volume service without compromising drink quality.

‍

Culinary Grade: Made for the Kitchen, Not the Cup

‍

Culinary matcha is made for food manufacturing and baking applications. The leaves are from later harvests, the tannin levels are higher, and the flavor is stronger and sometimes more bitter. The color tends toward a more muted or yellow-green tone. It's typically ground to a coarser particle size than drink-grade matcha.

‍

In baking, all of these "lower quality" characteristics are either neutralized or turned into advantages. Sugar balances the bitterness. Fat carries and amplifies the flavor. The coarser grind holds up well in bread and cake applications. Culinary grade is the right choice for matcha cookies, cakes, chocolates, ice cream, protein bars, granolas, pasta, and any recipe where matcha is an ingredient in a complex formulation.

‍

How to Choose the Right Grade for Your Business

‍

The honest answer is: it depends on what you're making. A simple framework:

If you're running a café and your primary matcha application is lattes, start with latte grade. If you want to offer a premium alternative or a traditional matcha bowl, add ceremonial grade. If you're doing any baking in your café, like matcha croissants, matcha cookies or matcha soft-serve then culinary grade is ideal for those applications.

‍

If you're a food manufacturer using matcha as a functional ingredient in a formulation, culinary grade is almost always the right choice. If you're creating a premium health product where the matcha is front and center, a higher-grade latte or ceremonial matcha may be worth the cost for the marketing story it enables.

‍

For bulk matcha wholesale at commercial volumes, the grade selection should be driven by application, not just price. Choosing the wrong grade costs you more in customer experience and product quality than any price saving justifies.

‍

Practical Tips for Each Grade in Operation

‍

Ceremonial grade: store in a cool, dark place in airtight packaging. Use within four to six weeks of opening for peak flavor. Portion into small working quantities and keep bulk stock sealed. Serve at water temperatures no higher than 70°C.

‍

Latte grade: your everyday workhorse. Batch paste preparation works well for busy service periods. Use within six to eight weeks of opening. Test color and flavor regularly to catch any degradation from improper storage.

‍

Culinary grade: the most forgiving of the three in terms of storage and handling. Still benefits from sealed, cool storage. For large-batch baking, weigh carefully — the stronger flavor means it's easy to over-dose and end up with an unpleasantly bitter product.

‍

Sample All Three Grades and Decide for Yourself

‍

Reading about matcha grades is useful. Tasting them is essential. The differences between grades are tangible and immediate — you'll notice the color, the aroma, and the flavor difference from the first comparison.

‍

We supply businesses across Europe with consistently sourced, clearly graded matcha with full traceability to Japanese origin. Find the grade (or grades) that work for your menu and your production, and build a reliable supply relationship from there.

Why Choosing the Right Matcha for Lattes Actually Matters

‍

If you run a café or develop beverages for a food brand, you've probably already learned that not every matcha powder performs the same way in a latte. Some powders produce a stunning vivid green. Others turn a dull, unappetizing khaki within minutes. Some hold up under oat milk with a clean, pleasant flavor. Others taste flat, bitter, or like the bottom of a garden bed.

‍

The market is flooded with matcha options right now — from bulk food-grade powders to premium ceremonial products that cost a small fortune. Navigating that landscape without wasting money on samples that don't work, or worse, without disappointing customers with a substandard drink, is one of the genuine challenges of menu development today.

‍

This guide cuts through the noise. We've evaluated matcha powders across the grades most relevant to latte applications, looking at color vibrancy, flavor under milk, dissolution, aroma, and value for volume use. Here's what we found.

‍

Grade 1: Latte Grade Matcha — The Professional Standard

‍

Latte grade matcha powder is the category built specifically for this job. Good latte grade matcha should hit every important metric for milk-based drinks: a vibrant medium-to-bright green color that holds under milk, a bold enough flavor to cut through oat or whole milk, good fine particle size for smooth suspension, and a price per gram that works at commercial scale.

‍

What to look for in a latte grade matcha: color that's rich green (not yellow-green, not brown-green), a fresh grassy-umami aroma when you open the bag, and a flavor that's assertive and clean with no harsh bitterness. The best latte grade matchas are sourced from Uji, Nishio, or Kagoshima regions in Japan and ground to a particle size fine enough to suspend evenly in liquid.

‍

For volume users, consistency across batches is arguably more important than peak quality in any single batch. A matcha that's spectacular in October and disappointing in February creates operational headaches and inconsistent customer experiences.

‍

Grade 2: Ceremonial Matcha — Premium Drinks and Purists

‍

Ceremonial matcha performs differently in lattes. The finer grind and higher-grade leaf profile mean it produces an extraordinarily smooth texture and a complex, naturally sweet flavor. In a milk-based drink, some of that nuance gets masked — but the color is typically exceptional, and the overall drinking experience is elevated.

‍

Some cafés deliberately use ceremonial grade matcha in lattes as a menu differentiator, positioning them as premium items at a higher price point. "Ceremonial matcha latte — made with first-harvest Uji matcha" is a menu description that commands a price premium and attracts serious matcha drinkers who notice the difference.

‍

The tradeoff is cost. Ceremonial matcha in volume is significantly more expensive than latte grade. If you're running 50+ matcha lattes a day, the economics may not work unless your selling price supports it. For lower-volume, premium-positioned venues, it can be a smart choice.

‍

Grade 3: Culinary Matcha — When and Why to Avoid It in Lattes

Culinary matcha is designed for baking, cooking, and manufacturing applications where other strong flavors and ingredients are present. It's typically made from later harvest leaves with a higher tannin content, producing a more robust and sometimes more bitter flavor. It's also generally a duller green color.

‍

In baking, those characteristics are advantages. You can use less of it to get green color and flavor, and any slight bitterness gets rounded out by sugar and fat. In a latte, those same characteristics become problems. The color can look muddy, the flavor can be flat or harsh, and the overall drink quality will disappoint customers who've had a well-made matcha latte before.

‍

Culinary matcha is appropriate for baking matcha pastries, making matcha glazes, or producing food products. It's a poor choice for the beverage menu. The cost savings over latte grade are rarely worth the quality difference in drink form.

‍

What Testing Shows: Performance Under Milk

‍

Testing matcha powders in latte conditions means looking at a few specific things. Color retention is how vibrant the green looks when combined with steamed milk — a good matcha latte should have a clear green tone. Flavor persistence is whether you can actually taste the matcha through the milk at a standard dose of 2–3 grams. Dissolution quality is how smoothly the powder integrates.

‍

Latte grade matcha consistently outperforms on all these measures when used as intended. Ceremonial grade wins on color and texture. Culinary grade underperforms on color and flavor in drink applications. The middle ground — a well-sourced, properly spec'd latte grade powder — is the sweet spot for commercial latte programs.

‍

How to Test Matcha Before You Buy in Volume

‍

Never commit to a large order of any matcha without testing it first. The evaluation process should include: a dry assessment (open the bag, check color and aroma), a hot water whisk test (3g in 60ml water at 70°C, check color, texture, and flavor), a milk test (the same paste topped with your standard steamed milk), and a cold preparation test if you serve iced matcha lattes.

‍

Run these tests with your whole team if possible. The person making drinks daily will notice things you might miss in a quick tasting. And taste against your current matcha if you have one — the comparison is often more telling than the absolute assessment.

‍

Check out wholesale pricing once you've identified the right grade, and make sure volume pricing works for your projected monthly usage.

‍

Our Recommendation for Café and Beverage Operators

‍

For most cafés and hospitality operators, a premium latte grade matcha from a reputable Japanese source — consistently spec'd, freshly packed, and available at commercial volume — is the right call. It outperforms on the metrics that matter in drink service and satisfies modern customers who have increasingly sophisticated matcha expectations.

‍

If your menu strategy supports a premium tier, consider stocking both latte grade and ceremonial matcha — one for everyday drinks and one for a premium menu position.

The Basics: What Is Hojicha?

If you've been exploring Japanese teas beyond matcha, you've likely come across hojicha — and if you haven't, it's worth your full attention. Hojicha (also spelled houjicha) is a Japanese green tea that has been roasted over charcoal or in a porcelain pot at high temperatures. That roasting process is what sets it entirely apart from every other Japanese green tea, including matcha.

‍

While most Japanese green teas are defined by their steaming or shading methods — processes designed to preserve green color and fresh, grassy flavors — hojicha goes in the opposite direction. The roasting transforms the leaves from green to a rich reddish-brown, and the flavor shifts from fresh and vegetal to warm, toasty, nutty, and caramel-like. It's a fundamentally different sensory experience, and one that has earned hojicha a devoted following well beyond Japan.

‍

Where Does Hojicha Come From?

Hojicha originated in Kyoto in the 1920s, when a tea merchant began roasting bancha (a common, coarser leaf tea) as a way to use leaves that were considered lower quality or unsellable in their unroasted state. What he discovered was that the roasting process didn't just salvage those leaves — it transformed them into something genuinely delicious.

‍

The stems, stalks, and leaves used in hojicha are typically from later harvests, often the third or fourth flush of the season. These more mature leaves have less l-theanine and more tannins in their raw state, but roasting mellows the tannins and brings out a complex, caramelized sweetness. Today, premium hojicha is also made from first-flush leaves and high-quality stems specifically selected for roasting.

‍

For powder applications — the form most relevant to cafés and food businesses — the roasted leaves are ground into a fine powder in the same way that matcha is produced. This hojicha powder wholesale is what you'll use for lattes, baked goods, desserts, and other applications.

‍

What Does Hojicha Taste Like?

This is where hojicha wins over people who find matcha too intense. The flavor profile is warm, roasty, and smooth. Think toasted grain, light caramel, a hint of wood smoke, and a gentle sweetness — all without the grassiness or bitterness that some drinkers associate with green tea.

‍

Hojicha is considerably lower in caffeine than matcha or most other teas, because the roasting process degrades caffeine content significantly. This makes it an excellent option for evening drinks, for customers who are caffeine-sensitive, and for children's menus or family-oriented café concepts.

‍

The roasted quality also means hojicha pairs extremely well with milk. A hojicha latte is warm, cozy, and deeply comforting — often compared to a hot chocolate in terms of its comfort-food appeal, but with a much cleaner, more sophisticated flavor profile.

‍

Hojicha vs. Matcha: The Key Differences

Both hojicha powder and matcha are made from ground Japanese tea leaves, but they're very different products. Matcha is made from shade-grown, unroasted green tea leaves and has a fresh, grassy, umami flavor with a vibrant green color. Hojicha is made from roasted leaves and has a warm, toasty flavor and a brown color.

‍

The caffeine levels differ significantly: matcha contains roughly 35mg of caffeine per gram, while hojicha powder contains much less, often around 7–10mg per gram. That's a meaningful difference for customers thinking about their daily caffeine intake.

‍

Taste-wise, matcha tends to appeal to customers who enjoy bold, complex, slightly bitter flavors with depth. Hojicha appeals to those who prefer warmth, sweetness, and roasted notes. Many cafés find that stocking both gives them coverage across a wider range of customer preferences and daypart occasions.

‍

Our matcha grades guide has more detail on how matcha grades work, if you want to go deeper on the matcha side of things.

‍

How to Use Hojicha Powder in Your Café

The most popular application is the hojicha latte. Use 2–3 grams of hojicha powder, whisk with a small amount of hot water (70–80°C) into a smooth paste, then top with steamed milk. The higher temperature tolerance of hojicha means you can use slightly hotter water without affecting the flavor negatively.

‍

Beyond lattes, hojicha powder opens up a wide range of menu options. Iced hojicha lattes are popular in summer months. Hojicha hot chocolate — made by whisking hojicha into a chocolate or cocoa base — is a genuinely compelling autumn drink. Hojicha is also brilliant in baking: hojicha cookies, hojicha buttercream frosting, hojicha cheesecake, and hojicha tiramisu all work beautifully because the roasty flavor plays well with sugar, butter, and chocolate.

‍

For food manufacturers, Hojicha Japan Organic is a compelling ingredient option for granola, protein bars, ice cream flavors, and premium beverage RTD products. The flavor profile differentiates product lines without requiring the consumer education that matcha sometimes needs.

‍

Sourcing Hojicha Powder for Your Business

Quality varies significantly between hojicha powders on the market. The key things to look for are: color consistency (a rich reddish-brown, not pale or khaki), aroma (strong roasted notes when you open the bag), flavor balance (warm and sweet, not bitter or stale), and particle size (fine enough to suspend smoothly in liquid without excessive clumping).

‍

Organic certification matters to many café customers and food brands today. Sourcing from certified organic Japanese farms also ensures you're not introducing agri-chemical residues into your recipes — something increasingly important for premium menu positioning.

fieldData.blog-summary: Everything baristas need to know about choosing and using matcha powder for lattes: grades, technique, dosing, and how to avoid the most common mistakes.
fieldData.blog-post-body:
What Makes Matcha Powder Different from Regular Tea?

Walk into any specialty café today and you'll find matcha on the menu. But not all matcha powder is created equal — and if you're behind the bar, that difference shows up immediately in the cup. Unlike loose-leaf green tea, matcha is made from shade-grown tea leaves that are stone-ground into a fine, vibrant powder. When you add liquid, you're consuming the whole leaf, not just an infusion. That's why it has such a distinct flavor profile: grassy, umami-forward, slightly sweet when high quality, and slightly bitter when it isn't.

For baristas, understanding the fundamentals of matcha powder sets you apart. You're not just scooping green powder into a cup — you're working with a product that has centuries of Japanese craftsmanship behind it, and one that customers increasingly know a lot about. Getting it right earns you repeat business. Getting it wrong loses you those customers to the café down the street.

The Two Types of Matcha You'll Actually Use Behind the Bar

There's an important distinction every barista needs to understand: ceremonial grade and latte grade matcha are different products designed for different applications.

Ceremonial matcha is the top tier. It's made from the youngest, most tender leaves of the first harvest — called ichibancha — and ground to an ultra-fine, silk-like powder. The color is a vivid, electric green. The flavor is naturally sweet, mellow, and complex. Traditionally, ceremonial matcha is whisked with hot water alone, no milk, no sweetener. It's meant to be tasted as it is. Some cafés serve it as a traditional bowl or as a premium straight matcha shot, and it works beautifully in that context.

Latte grade matcha is what most baristas will reach for every day. It's specifically designed to hold its flavor and color when mixed with milk. The flavor profile is bolder and slightly more robust, which means it doesn't get lost under oat milk or steamed whole milk. It's harvested from slightly more mature leaves, usually from later flushes, giving it more structure and a stronger, more assertive green tea character. And because it's used in larger quantities per drink, the price point is significantly more accessible for high-volume café use.

Using ceremonial matcha in a latte isn't necessarily wrong, but it's an expensive choice where the nuances of that premium product get masked by milk. Using culinary or food-grade matcha in drinks often produces a dull, khaki-green color and a flat or bitter taste. Latte grade hits the sweet spot.

How to Whisk Matcha Like a Professional

The technique matters as much as the product. Here's the standard process used by professional baristas:

Start with 2–3 grams of latte grade matcha powder per serving. Sift the powder into your bowl or pitcher using a small fine-mesh sieve — this breaks up clumps and ensures a smoother suspension. Add a small amount of hot water, around 60–70°C. Boiling water scorches the chlorophyll and makes matcha taste bitter and flat. You want it hot enough to hydrate the powder fully, not so hot it damages the flavor.

Whisk vigorously using a bamboo chasen or a small electric frother. The goal is a smooth, lump-free paste first, then a thin, even liquid. You should see a fine foam on top with no visible powder clumps. Then add your steamed milk — oat, almond, whole, or whatever your customer prefers.

The paste method works well for high-volume service. Pre-mix a small batch of matcha paste at the start of service and keep it at room temperature. When an order comes in, portion your paste into the cup and top with steamed milk. This is faster and more consistent than whisking to order every time.

Common Matcha Latte Mistakes (And How to Fix Them)

Clumping is the number one complaint. It happens when you add cold or room-temperature liquid directly to dry powder, or when you skip the sifting step. Always sift and always start with a small amount of hot water to form a paste before adding the rest of your liquid.

Bitter taste usually means the water was too hot. Drop your water temperature to 65°C and taste again. If bitterness persists, check the quality of your matcha — older or lower-grade powder can be inherently bitter regardless of water temperature.

Color that looks army green or brownish rather than vibrant green is a sign of oxidized or low-grade matcha. Good latte grade matcha should be a rich, medium-to-bright green. Store your matcha in an airtight container, away from light and heat, and use it within six to eight weeks of opening.

Weak flavor in a milk-based drink often means you're under-dosing. Milk dilutes and coats the palate, so you generally need more matcha per cup than you might expect. Start at 2.5 grams and taste up from there.

Dosing Guide for Café Use

Consistency is everything in a professional café environment. Here's a simple dosing framework:

A standard matcha latte (12 oz) works well with 2–3 grams of latte grade matcha. An iced matcha latte benefits from slightly more — 3–4 grams — because ice dilutes the drink. A matcha shot typically uses 4–5 grams. Specialty drinks like matcha dirty lattes or matcha smoothies can use 2–3 grams since other strong flavors are present.

Train your team to use a calibrated scoop or digital scale rather than eyeballing. Inconsistency in matcha dosing is one of the fastest ways to generate customer complaints about a drink tasting different on different days.

Choosing the Right Matcha Supplier for Your Café

Once you've dialed in your technique, the supplier relationship becomes your most important variable. You want a supplier who can guarantee consistent flavor profile and color across every batch, offer food-safe sourcing with traceability to origin, provide reliable stock for your volume needs, and give you flexible ordering options as your business grows.

For matcha for cafés specifically, working with a B2B-focused supplier rather than a retail brand makes a significant difference. Wholesale suppliers understand your operational needs — bulk packaging, consistent spec sheets, and responsive service when you're about to run out mid-week.

Pure Matcha Partners sources directly from Japan, with full traceability from farm to bag. The latte grade and ceremonial ranges are clearly differentiated, consistently spec'd, and available at wholesale volumes that work for independent cafés and multi-location groups alike.

Start with a Sample Before You Commit

The best way to find your café's signature matcha is to taste it. Different latte grade matchas have meaningfully different flavor profiles — some more grassy, some more umami, some with a mild sweetness. There's no substitute for putting the powder in a cup and drinking it.

Request a free sample from Pure Matcha Partners and taste the difference for yourself. We ship samples to cafés and hospitality businesses across Europe with no obligation. Get your team involved, run a tasting, and choose the matcha your customers will keep coming back for.
